Yes, weak limits are unique: $v = w$.

**Proof.** Suppose $\{v_n\}$ converges weakly to both $v$ and $w$ in the normed linear space $V$. By definition of weak convergence, for every continuous linear functional $f \in V^*$, we have
$$f(v_n) \to f(v) \quad \text{and} \quad f(v_n) \to f(w).$$
Since $\{f(v_n)\}$ is a sequence of scalars converging in $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$), and scalar limits are unique, it follows that
$$f(v) = f(w) \quad \text{for every } f \in V^*.$$

It remains to show that $f(v) = f(w)$ for all $f \in V^*$ implies $v = w$. This is precisely the content of the **Hahn–Banach separation theorem** (a corollary of the Hahn–Banach theorem): if $v \neq w$, then $v - w \neq 0$, and there exists a continuous linear functional $f \in V^*$ with $f(v - w) \neq 0$, i.e., $f(v) \neq f(w)$.

Concretely, on the one-dimensional subspace $\operatorname{span}\{v-w\}$, define $g(\alpha(v-w)) = \alpha\|v-w\|$. This is a bounded linear functional with $\|g\| = 1$. By the Hahn–Banach theorem, $g$ extends to some $f \in V^*$ with $\|f\| = 1$. Then
$$f(v) - f(w) = f(v-w) = g(v-w) = \|v-w\| \neq 0,$$
contradicting $f(v) = f(w)$ for all $f \in V^*$.

Therefore $v = w$, and weak limits in a normed linear space are unique. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
